title: Oil Prices Climb as Saudi Pipeline Outage and Houthi Advances Deepen Supply Fears
excerpt: Brent crude traded near $108 a barrel on Tuesday as the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and fresh Houthi attacks on the kingdom compounded fears of a prolonged supply squeeze.
body:
• Brent crude rose to about $108 a barrel on Tuesday as traders priced in prolonged supply disruption after attacks knocked Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline offline.
  • The 750-mile pipeline, which carries 4 to 5 million barrels a day to the Red Sea, allows the kingdom to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz; partial operations may resume within days but full repairs could take six to eight weeks.
  • Houthi seizures of Perim Island and the port of Mokha are threatening Red Sea shipping at the Bab el-Mandeb strait, while Hormuz vessel traffic has fallen to fewer than 10 transits a day.
  • The surge is feeding inflation fears ahead of this week's Fed meeting, with US gasoline at $4.36 a gallon and diesel at a record $6.23.

Oil prices climbed on Tuesday as concerns over supply disruptions persisted after attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure left the kingdom's East-West pipeline offline and cast doubt on efforts to ease shipping risks in the Gulf.

Brent crude futures rose 1.8% to $107.59 a barrel in early European trading, while US West Texas Intermediate gained 1.9% to $103.30, according to the Wall Street Journal. Prices remained below Monday's intraday highs, when Brent briefly reached $109.80 and WTI touched $104.35 before paring gains. Brent settled at $105.68 on Monday, its highest closing level since May, after surging 4.4% on the day and 8.7% last week.

The pipeline attack

Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West pipeline late Friday after drone attacks that both Riyadh and Baghdad said originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response. The Saudi energy ministry said the pipeline's pumping stations in the Riyadh and Medina regions were struck on Thursday, and the line was closed as a precaution.

The 1,200-kilometer pipeline is the biggest in the Middle East and the kingdom's key workaround for the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively blockaded since the US-Iran war began on February 28. It can carry as much as 7 million barrels a day from the eastern oil-producing region to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and had been moving 4 to 5 million barrels a day in recent months, equivalent to 4% to 5% of global supply.

Saudi Arabia is trying to resume partial operations within days, though damaged pumping stations could take six to eight weeks to fully repair, the Wall Street Journal reported. Analysts warn the outage could force Saudi Arabia to cut output as storage fills.

"Supply is becoming a prized commodity, and without greater clarity on where replacement barrels will come from, we wouldn't be surprised to see prices push higher in the short term."

— Janiv Shah, analyst at Rystad Energy

Red Sea pressure builds

Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia on Monday, firing missiles and drones at the Khamis Mushait military airbase in southern Saudi Arabia in retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen.

Over the weekend the Houthis seized Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, after taking the nearby port of Mokha, further threatening oil flows through the Red Sea corridor. Commodity vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to fewer than 10 transits a day over the weekend from a 10-day average of 14, and planned talks between Gulf Arab states and Iran on opening the strait were postponed.

"Oil traders are treating every fresh attack or infrastructure hit as incremental supply risk, while staying highly sensitive to any sign that the East-West pipeline or Hormuz flows could normalise."

— Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade

Inflation and the Fed

The rally is inflaming inflation fears just as the Federal Reserve begins its two-day meeting. US gasoline reached $4.36 a gallon on Monday, up 6% from a month ago and 36% higher than a year ago, according to AAA data.

Commonwealth Bank of Australia's Vivek Dhar said global crude and refined-product inventories now provide only five to 11 weeks of cover as the market's cushions weaken. Analysts at RBC Capital Markets tipped Brent could hit $121.99 in the fourth quarter, and Goldman Sachs and HSBC have raised their crude price forecasts for the rest of 2026 and 2027.

Diaspora Angle

For US households, the spike lands directly at the pump and in heating and grocery bills, while energy-heavy portfolios and 401(k)s get a lift — a reminder to check how much of a household's exposure rides on fuel prices.

What's Next

The market's next signal comes from the pipeline itself: whether Saudi Arabia restores partial operations within days as planned, or whether repairs drag on and force deeper export cuts. Traders will also watch the Fed's Wednesday decision for any hint that oil-driven inflation is hardening the case for rate hikes.
